note: The plesiomorphic locomotor engine of the vertebrate body (Schilling 2011). Two divisions separated by the horizontal septum and marked by the split of the spinal nerve: epaxial above, on dorsal rami; hypaxial below, on ventral rami. That nerve boundary is the same kind of evidence that anchors the dorsal/ventral limb masses, and it is why axial muscles belong in this dataset rather than beside it — the appendicular system is built on top of the axial one and takes over from it.

muscles.name: Epaxial musculature
muscles.developmental: Somitic (primaxial); myotome dorsal to the horizontal septum. Innervated by the DORSAL rami of the spinal nerves — the defining criterion.

consensus.origin: Neural spines, transverse processes, zygapophyses and the vertebral centra; in fishes, the myosepta.
consensus.insertion: Successive vertebrae, ribs and the skull; the tracts span many segments in amniotes.
consensus.action: Plesiomorphically mobilisation — lateral bending for swimming. In tetrapods it additionally stabilises the trunk against inertial and limb-muscle forces; in mammals it also serves sagittal mobility and stabilises against the inertia of the body's centre of mass.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Myomeric axial musculature
occurrences.note: Segmental myomeres separated by myosepta, undivided into tracts. Axial-based locomotion in its plesiomorphic form.

occurrences.name: Epaxial myomeres
occurrences.note: Divided from the hypaxial by the horizontal septum, but still strictly segmental.

occurrences.name: Dorsalis trunci
occurrences.note: Retains much of the segmental fish arrangement; lateral undulation still contributes to locomotion alongside the limbs.

occurrences.name: Dorsalis trunci
occurrences.note: Greatly shortened with the reduced presacral column and the urostyle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Discoglossus and Ascaphus, from Prikryl et al.'s review table and descriptions. Longissimus dorsi, from the sacral and presacral vertebrae onto the urostyle, rotating it dorsally. In anurans the epaxial series has been rebuilt around a rigid trunk and a rod: it moves one bone rather than bending a column.

occurrences.name: Transversospinalis, longissimus, iliocostalis
occurrences.note: Reorganised into three longitudinal, polysegmental tracts — the amniote condition. Cieri (2018) documents the regionalisation along the varanid column.

occurrences.name: Epaxial tracts (reduced)
occurrences.note: Much reduced with the rigid synsacrum and shortened tail.

occurrences.name: Transversospinal system, longissimus, iliocostalis
occurrences.origin: Neural spines, transverse processes and the sacrum.
occurrences.insertion: Successive vertebrae, ribs and the occiput.
occurrences.action: Stabilises the trunk against sagittal components of limb-muscle action; permits and controls the sagittal bending of the mammalian back.
occurrences.note: The transversospinal muscle is further subdivided into the transversospinal system (multifidus, semispinalis and relatives). Schilling ties this to the evolution of a mobile lumbar region and a rib-free lumbar segment.

homology.notes: Epaxial identity is defined by position dorsal to the horizontal septum and by dorsal-ramus innervation, both of which hold from lampreys to mammals. The three amniote tracts are a reorganisation within that field, not new muscles. Schilling maps the character states onto a phylogeny and infers the ancestral condition at each node.
homology.teaching: The clearest case that innervation defines a muscle field: the dorsal/ventral ramus split is the same logic as the dorsal/ventral limb masses, and it is visible in a single cross-section.

muscles.name: Hypaxial musculature
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome ventral to the horizontal septum. Innervated by the VENTRAL rami of the spinal nerves. The abaxial part of this field is what migrates into the limb bud and becomes the appendicular musculature.

consensus.origin: Ventral surfaces of the vertebrae, the ribs, and the pelvic girdle.
consensus.insertion: Ribs, sternum, linea alba and the pelvic girdle.
consensus.action: Lateral bending in fishes; in tetrapods, trunk stabilisation, ventilation and support of the viscera against gravity.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Abdominal wall + subvertebral musculature
occurrences.note: How the hypaxial mass is apportioned tracks habitat across urodeles. Omura et al. weighed every trunk muscle in five species and found the lateral hypaxial layers taking roughly a quarter of trunk muscle mass each in the aquatic Amphiuma and Necturus against under a tenth in the terrestrial Hynobius and Ambystoma, with the rectus abdominis running the other way. The subvertebral portion rises with terrestriality alongside the epaxial mass. Proportions, not attachments — the sample is five species and three habitat classes, so it constrains what the hypaxial mass is FOR without saying where any part of it inserts.

occurrences.name: Subvertebralis, obliquus externus/internus, transversus abdominis, rectus abdominis, intercostales
occurrences.note: Cieri (2018) records the regional differentiation of these along the varanid trunk, which bears on how much of lateral undulation survives alongside limb-driven locomotion.

occurrences.name: Quadratus lumborum, psoas minor, obliquus externus/internus, transversus abdominis, rectus abdominis, intercostales
occurrences.action: The rectus abdominis is the most important sagittal flexor of the mammalian trunk; the subvertebral muscles are correlated with the evolution of a mobile lumbar region.

homology.notes: Ventral-ramus innervation is the constant. The important connection for this dataset is developmental: the abaxial portion of the hypaxial field is the source of the appendicular musculature, so the limb muscles are hypaxial derivatives that migrated out. That is why the limb's ventral (flexor) mass keeps ventral-division nerves.
homology.teaching: Answers the question students ask once they meet the dorsal/ventral limb masses: where did those masses come from? They are the hypaxial field, migrated.

muscles.name: Caudal musculature
muscles.developmental: Somitic; the post-sacral continuation of the epaxial and hypaxial series.

consensus.origin: Caudal vertebrae — their centra, neural spines, transverse processes and haemal arches.
consensus.insertion: Successive caudal vertebrae; the caudofemoralis leaves the series to insert on the femur.
consensus.action: Tail movement; in taxa with a large tail, also counterbalance and — through the caudofemoralis — femoral retraction.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal and ventral rami of the caudal spinal nerves.

occurrences.note: Lost with the tail; the urostyle replaces the caudal series.

occurrences.name: Caudal musculature (ilio-, ischio- and caudofemoralis series)
occurrences.note: Tomańska et al. (2024) describe the Komodo dragon tail as a substantial locomotor and defensive organ, with caudal muscle mass contributing counterbalance during bipedal rearing.

occurrences.name: Caudal musculature (reduced)
occurrences.note: Reduced to the pygostyle and its rectricial muscles.
Retained in taxa with a muscular tail, reduced in others.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The sacrocaudalis series, dorsal and ventral, medial and lateral. The dorsalis medialis is the caudal continuation of the transversospinalis: its most cranial bundle arises from the caudal and dorsal spinous process of the last lumbar vertebra, subsequent bundles from the sacral and caudal spinous processes, inserting on the cranial ends of the anterior articular processes of caudal vertebrae. Each bundle spans about three vertebrae.

homology.notes: The caudal series is the post-sacral continuation of the trunk musculature. Its interest for this dataset is the caudofemoralis, which leaves the axial series to reach the femur and so becomes an abaxial, appendicular muscle — the one muscle that crosses the boundary this file is organised around.
homology.teaching: Pair with the caudofemoralis and the fourth trochanter: the tail powers the hindlimb in most tetrapods, and both bird and mammal locomotion required breaking that link.

muscles.name: Longissimus dorsi
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome dorsal to the horizontal septum, on the dorsal rami.

consensus.origin: Transverse processes and the ilium, spanning many segments.
consensus.insertion: Transverse processes and ribs of more cranial vertebrae; the skull in some taxa.
consensus.action: Lateral bending and, in mammals, sagittal extension; trunk stabilisation.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: M. longissimus dorsi
occurrences.note: Cieri (2018) refers the detailed attachment tendons of longissimus, transversospinalis and iliocostalis to Gasc (1981), Ritter (1995) and Tsuihiji (2007) rather than redescribing them.

homology.notes: One of the three longitudinal epaxial tracts of amniotes. The aponeurosis dividing it from the iliocostalis is itself a muscle attachment site in varanids — it carries the supracostalis dorsus brevis.

muscles.name: Iliocostalis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome dorsal to the horizontal septum, on the dorsal rami.

consensus.insertion: Ribs and transverse processes of more cranial vertebrae.
consensus.action: Lateral bending; rib and trunk stabilisation.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: M. iliocostalis
occurrences.note: Cieri (2018) describes it as very thin in Varanus exanthematicus.

homology.notes: The most lateral of the three epaxial tracts.

muscles.name: Transversospinalis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome dorsal to the horizontal septum, on the dorsal rami.

consensus.insertion: Neural spines of more cranial vertebrae.
consensus.action: Extension and rotation of the vertebral column; segmental stabilisation.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Transversospinal system (multifidus, semispinalis and relatives)
occurrences.note: Subdivided into several entities in mammals; Schilling (2011) ties that subdivision to the evolution of a mobile, rib-free lumbar region.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Lumbar sector only. The medialmost epaxial series, metameres largely fused with each other and with the thoracic continuation, from the lateral spinous processes and dorsal articular processes of all lumbar vertebrae but the last, plus the lumbodorsal fascia, onto the mammillary processes of the lumbar vertebrae and, for the last bundle, the intermediate sacral crest of S1-2. It is continuous caudally with the sacrocaudalis dorsalis medialis, which is why the tail and the back are one series and not two.

homology.notes: The medial epaxial tract, and the one that elaborates most in mammals.

muscles.name: Supracostalis dorsus brevis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome dorsal to the horizontal septum, on the dorsal rami.

consensus.origin: The aponeurosis dividing the longissimus from the iliocostalis.
consensus.insertion: Dorsal aspect of each dorsal rib, one- to two-thirds of the way down its length.
consensus.action: Lifts each rib independently of its neighbours. Cieri (2018) positions it to produce caliper motion of the ribs — rotation about a dorsoventral axis.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: M. supracostalis dorsus brevis
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal aspect of each dorsal rib, one- to two-thirds down its length.
occurrences.note: Segmentally divided into triangular sheets; strongly developed in Varanus exanthematicus. Its insertion tendons are continuous with those of the obliquus externus superficialis.

homology.notes: One of two muscles Cieri (2018) finds in Varanus exanthematicus and NOT in Iguana iguana, the other being the levator costae. Both take origin from the vertebral column or its fascia rather than from adjacent ribs, so each rib can be moved independently — a different mechanical arrangement from the rib-to-rib intercostal series.
homology.openQuestion: Whether these two muscles are varanid novelties or more widely distributed among squamates is open; Cieri notes that basic body-wall muscle descriptions are lacking for most reptiles.
homology.teaching: A concrete case where adding a muscle changes what the skeleton can do: rib-to-vertebra muscles allow independent rib motion that rib-to-rib muscles cannot.

muscles.name: Levator costae
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome ventral to the horizontal septum, on the ventral rami.

consensus.insertion: Fanning out onto the proximal part of the articulating rib.
consensus.action: Elevates each rib relative to its own vertebra.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: M. levator costae
occurrences.note: A small muscle deep to the longissimus dorsi and the external intercostal, connecting each rib to its articulating vertebra. Absent in Iguana iguana.

homology.notes: The hypaxial counterpart of the supracostalis dorsus brevis, and the second of the two muscles Cieri finds in Varanus but not Iguana. Note the pair straddles the horizontal septum: one epaxial on dorsal rami, one hypaxial on ventral rami, doing mechanically similar jobs.
homology.teaching: Two muscles with the same mechanical role on opposite sides of the epaxial/hypaxial boundary — a reminder that the division is developmental and neural, not functional.

muscles.name: Obliquus externus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome ventral to the horizontal septum, on the ventral rami.

consensus.origin: Margin between the rectus abdominis lateralis and ventralis.
consensus.insertion: Lateral aspect of the dorsal ribs, about a third of the way down, by short tendons.
consensus.action: Compresses the body wall; contributes to ventilation and trunk stabilisation.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: M. obliquus externus (superficialis + profundus)
occurrences.note: Well developed in Varanus exanthematicus. The superficialis covers the lateral body wall; its insertion tendons are continuous with those of the supracostalis dorsus brevis, so the epaxial and hypaxial sheets meet at the rib.

occurrences.name: Obliquus externus
occurrences.insertion: A midline aponeurosis crossing deep to the rectus abdominis.
occurrences.action: Resists long-axis torsion generated by limb support during walking; bends the body during swimming.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fibres run dorsoanterior to ventroposterior at about 50 degrees to the body axis. Neither end reaches bone — both attachments are fascial, which is why the layer leaves no osteological correlate.

parts.name: Obliquus externus superficialis
parts.note: Present as a distinct layer in Amphiuma, Cynops and Ambystoma; absent as such in Necturus and Hynobius, where the external oblique is undivided.

occurrences.divisionNote: Omura et al. dissected five urodeles of three habitat types and found the external oblique undivided in Necturus maculosus and Hynobius nigrescens but split into a superficialis and a profundus in Amphiuma tridactylum, Cynops pyrrhogaster and Ambystoma tigrinum. The whole lateral hypaxial stack likewise runs to two, three or four layers depending on species. The split does not track habitat — one aquatic and one terrestrial species share the undivided condition — so it is polymorphic within Caudata rather than a functional grade, and scoring the clade from any one exemplar would manufacture a transition.
occurrences.note: Fibre angle is measured, not estimated: roughly 50 degrees to the body axis against roughly 145 degrees for the internal oblique, so the two layers cross at close to a right angle.

homology.notes: Outermost of the four body-wall layers Cieri (2018) recognises: obliquus externus, intercostales externi, intercostales interni, transversus, from superficial to deep.

muscles.name: Intercostales externi
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome ventral to the horizontal septum, on the ventral rami.

consensus.insertion: Caudal aspect of the next most cranial rib.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Mm. intercostales externi
occurrences.note: Fibres course dorsocranially at about 15° above the long axis of the body, covering the costal cartilages of the floating ribs and the dorsal third of the sternal portion of each true rib.

homology.notes: Rib-to-rib, unlike the levator costae and supracostalis dorsus brevis, which run rib-to-vertebra. Cieri's fibre-angle measurements (about 15° here against about 60° for the interni) are what distinguish the two layers.

muscles.name: Intercostales interni
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome ventral to the horizontal septum, on the ventral rami.

consensus.origin: Cranial aspect of each dorsal rib.
consensus.insertion: Sternocostal joints in the region of the true ribs; ventral aspect of each floating rib.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Mm. intercostales interni
occurrences.note: Course caudodorsally at about 60° above the long axis between the dorsal ribs, and parallel to it between the sternal segments of the true ribs.

homology.notes: Third of the four body-wall layers.

muscles.name: Transversus abdominis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome ventral to the horizontal septum, on the ventral rami.

consensus.origin: Medial fascia deep to the sternum, and the fascia at the lateral margin of the rectus abdominis caudal to the sternum.
consensus.insertion: Cranial aspect of the ventral quarter of the vertebral portion of each bipartite dorsal rib; the lumbodorsal fascia caudal to those ribs.
consensus.action: Compresses the abdomen; supports the viscera.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: M. transversus
occurrences.note: The deepest and thinnest of the body-wall muscles in Varanus exanthematicus.

occurrences.name: Transversus abdominis
occurrences.origin: Transverse processes of the trunk vertebrae.
occurrences.insertion: Crosses the ventral midline to the corresponding attachment of the opposite side.
occurrences.action: Resists long-axis torsion during walking, bends the body during swimming, and powers exhalation.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The deepest of the three oblique layers, with dorsoventral fibres. The only one of them reaching the vertebral column.

homology.notes: Deepest of the four body-wall layers.

muscles.name: Rectus abdominis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome ventral to the horizontal septum, on the ventral rami.

consensus.origin: Pubis and the ventral pelvic girdle.
consensus.insertion: Sternum, costal cartilages and the linea alba.
consensus.action: Flexes the trunk. Schilling (2011) calls it the most important sagittal flexor of the mammalian trunk.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: M. rectus abdominis (ventralis + lateralis)
occurrences.note: Cieri (2018) distinguishes a main ventral belly from a superficial rectus abdominis lateralis; the margin between them carries the origin of the obliquus externus superficialis.

Separable as a discrete muscle only in the more terrestrial urodeles. Omura et al. could not distinguish it from the external and internal obliques in either aquatic species they dissected — Amphiuma tridactylum and Necturus maculosus — while it separated cleanly in the semi-aquatic Cynops and the terrestrial Hynobius and Ambystoma. It is also much the smallest share of trunk muscle mass in the aquatic species and the largest in the terrestrial ones, which is the load-bearing reading: a body held off the ground needs a ventral tie between the girdles, and a swimming one does not. The description below is Taricha torosa, where it is discrete.
occurrences.name: Rectus abdominis
occurrences.origin: Anterior border of the pubo-ischiac plate and the ypsiloid cartilage.
occurrences.insertion: Sternum and pericardium superficially; the deep portion runs on as the rectus cervicis profundus to the hyoid.
occurrences.action: Prevents the trunk sagging between the girdles during walking, and draws the pelvic and pectoral girdles toward each other.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Divided into superficial and deep portions, the halves separated at the midline by the linea alba and segmented by tendinous inscriptions. The lateral fibres of the superficial portion attach to the pectoralis rather than to bone, which is why the pectoralis takes part of its own origin from those inscriptions.

homology.notes: The ventral longitudinal member of the hypaxial series, outside the four transverse body-wall layers.

muscles.name: Obliquus internus
muscles.developmental: Hypaxial; lateral plate of the body wall, deep to the external oblique.

consensus.origin: Connective tissue deep to the obliquus externus.
consensus.action: Resists long-axis torsion generated by limb support; bends the body during swimming.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Obliquus internus
occurrences.origin: Connective tissue deep to the obliquus externus.
occurrences.insertion: An aponeurosis crossing the ventral midline.
occurrences.note: Fibres run ventroanterior to dorsoposterior at about 145 degrees to the body axis, close to perpendicular to those of the external oblique. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Neither attachment is skeletal. The middle of the three oblique layers, thinner than the external oblique.

homology.notes: The middle layer of the tetrapod body wall. The dataset previously carried the external oblique and the transversus but not the layer between them.

muscles.name: Ypsiloideus
muscles.developmental: Hypaxial; posterior continuation of the superficial rectus abdominis.

consensus.origin: Anterior edge of the medial pubis.
consensus.action: Assists the rectus abdominis in preventing the trunk from sagging.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the posterior trunk spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Ypsiloideus
occurrences.origin: Anterior edge of the medial pubis.
occurrences.note: Appears to be the posterior continuation of the part of the superficial rectus abdominis spanning ypsiloid cartilage and pelvic girdle, and is separated from it only formally. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Both attachments are on structures with no amniote counterpart — the ypsiloid cartilage is a salamander apomorphy, which is why this muscle has no homologue outside the group.

homology.notes: Tied to the ypsiloid cartilage and so restricted to salamanders. Whether it is a discrete muscle or a named part of the rectus abdominis is a matter of convention, as the paper concedes.
